subtitle: Encrypted messengers, calls and group chat.

subsections.title: Choosing a Tool
subsections.summary: What to look for in any messenger or email service.

items.title: Encrypted by default
items.html: End-to-end encryption should be on for every chat and call, not an option you have to find.

items.title: No phone number needed
items.html: A phone number ties an account to your real identity. Some apps work without one, or let you hide it behind a username.

items.title: Open source & audited
items.html: Public code and independent security audits mean you don’t have to take the company’s word for it.

items.title: Disappearing messages
items.html: Messages that delete themselves protect you if a phone is lost, seized or hacked later.

items.title: Little metadata
items.html: Even when content is encrypted, who you talk to and when can be revealing. Prefer services that keep as little as possible.

items.title: Who runs the server
items.html: For self-hosted and federated tools (Matrix, Jitsi, Mastodon), the person running your server can see more. Pick one you trust.

subsections.title: Messaging Apps
subsections.summary: Encrypted alternatives to WhatsApp and SMS.

items.label: Signal
items.desc: The easiest switch: feels like WhatsApp, encrypted by default, run by a non-profit. Needs a phone number but lets you hide it behind a username.

items.label: SimpleX Chat
items.desc: No phone number and no user ID at all — you connect through one-time invite links or QR codes.

items.label: Molly
items.desc: A hardened version of Signal for Android, with an encrypted local database and Tor support.

items.label: Session
items.desc: No phone number or email to sign up; messages travel over a decentralised network.

items.label: Threema
items.desc: Swiss messenger that needs no phone number. Paid once, no subscription.

items.label: Briar
items.desc: No servers: syncs phone-to-phone over Bluetooth, Wi-Fi or Tor, so it works even when the internet is down.

items.label: Delta Chat
items.desc: chat app that runs over ordinary email accounts.

items.label: Element
items.desc: app for Matrix, a federated, encrypted chat network for communities.

items.label: Jami
items.desc: peer-to-peer messaging and calls with no central server.

items.label: Tox
items.desc: peer-to-peer encrypted messaging and calling protocol.

items.label: XMPP
items.desc: open, decentralised chat standard; many apps support encryption.

items.label: Ricochet Refresh
items.desc: anonymous desktop messenger that runs over Tor.

items.label: OTR
items.desc: “Off-the-Record”, an older encryption protocol for desktop chat.

items.label: Telegram
items.desc: popular, but chats are not end-to-end encrypted unless you start a one-to-one “Secret Chat”.

blocks.label: WhatsApp & Telegram
blocks.html: WhatsApp encrypts message content but shares metadata with Meta. Telegram’s normal and group chats aren’t end-to-end encrypted, so Telegram itself can read them. Both are fine for public channels; use Signal or SimpleX for anything private.

subsections.title: Calls, Meetings & Group Chat
subsections.summary: Video calls and team chat you control.

items.label: Signal
items.desc: encrypted voice and video calls, including groups.

items.label: Jitsi Meet
items.desc: free, open-source video meetings in the browser — use a server whose operator you trust.

items.label: Mattermost
items.desc: self-hostable team chat, a Slack alternative.

items.label: Rocket.Chat
items.desc: self-hostable team chat with hosted plans.
